Decision: no roles eliminated; 100 people retrained and moved to plant roles at plant-role pay; 25 retrained and moved to plant roles keeping current pay.

Rationale. The 125 roles are no longer needed, and the $11.4 million annual saving is realized on every path. The question is how to treat the people. Eliminating roles ends pay for everyone affected. Even with modest severance, that is the outcome most harmful to employees and to the communities where they live, and it forgoes the value of people the Company is already hiring for. The plants hire about 500 people a year from outside into production, maintenance and warehouse roles that these employees can fill after retraining, so retraining both protects people and fills a real need.

Cost. Retraining costs $15,000 per person and the training period carries $45,600 in pay and benefits per person, about $7.6 million once for all 125. Each retrained person is an investment that pays back against outside hiring in two years. The cash needed is well within the $44.1 million above minimum operating cash, and the ongoing saving from removed work more than covers the pay-difference cost of the keep-pay group.

Pay. The plant-role pay path cuts pay sharply for business and financial operations staff (39.8%), so I have placed a smaller group of those employees on the keep-pay path at a cost of about $16,560 a year each, about $0.4 million a year for 25 people. The rest, mostly office and administrative staff whose pay change is only 1.5%, move at plant-role pay.

Trade-offs. The keep-pay path costs more and leaves the Company with an ongoing liability each year it is held, so I have limited it to the group facing the largest cut. Over the four-quarter horizon this balances employee security, community employment, customer service continuity, and shareholder cost. I will review the keep-pay group against plant vacancies at the next quarter.

I chose to redeploy all 125 affected people rather than eliminate any roles. The $11.4 million annual saving from the removed work is captured on every path, so the choice is about how people are treated, not whether the saving happens. Severance would end 125 incomes at once, at a cost to employees and their communities that outweighs the modest up-front saving of about $1.1 million versus $1.9 million of retraining, and it gives the Company no return from the people it has trained and knows.

Moving people into plant roles fills positions the Company would otherwise hire for from outside, about 500 a year, so retraining is an investment that pays back in about two years. The 80 people moved at plant pay are mainly office and administrative staff, whose pay falls only 1.5%, so the cost to them is small and they keep a job. For business and financial operations staff, the plant-role pay cut is 39.8%. I have kept 45 people on current pay for that reason. Their pay gap is about $16,560 a year each, roughly $0.7 million a year across the group, which is affordable and is a deliberate cost to shareholders in exchange for protecting employees from a steep loss of income.

Total one-time cost is about $7.6 million (retraining and training pay), with ongoing pay gap costs of about $0.7 million a year. Both are covered by the $44.1 million of cash above the minimum operating level, and the undrawn $300 million facility is available as a backstop. Cash flow after dividends and repurchases was positive, so the Company can absorb this within the year. The chosen mix respects customers (no disruption to plants or service), suppliers (no change to purchasing), the environment (no effect on compliance or projects), and shareholders (a modest, bounded cost with a two-year payback). Next quarter I will review the 45 pay-protected employees and whether some can transition to plant pay as the plant roles settle.

I chose to retrain all 125 affected people into plant roles rather than eliminate any role. The plants hire about 500 people a year from outside into production, maintenance and warehouse work, so these employees can fill openings the Company would otherwise fill by hiring, and no one is left without a livelihood. Severance alone would be the cheapest path, about $1.1 million, but it ends 125 careers and offers no route into the Company's own openings, which weighs heavily against the employee and community objectives.

I split the group between two retraining paths. 85 people move at plant-role pay. For office and administrative support staff this is a small change, a 1.5% reduction, and the retraining cost of $15,000 per person is recovered within two years compared with hiring from outside. 40 people move keeping their current pay, which protects business and financial operations staff from a cut of about 40%. The pay difference on this group is about $16,560 per person a year, roughly $0.66 million a year in total. That is a recurring cost, but it is small against $238.5 million of operating income and is affordable from the Company's existing cash flow after capital spending.

The one-time cost is about $1.9 million for instruction and materials, plus $5.7 million of pay and benefits during six months of training, which is paid from cash above the minimum operating level. The total saving of $11.4 million a year from the eliminated work is preserved on every path, since the work itself is no longer needed.

I did not eliminate roles because the board's objective covers employees and communities, not only shareholders. Retraining keeps experienced staff with the Company, avoids severance and disruption, and makes use of the plants' ongoing hiring need. I will monitor the retraining outcomes and the cost of the keep-pay group against plant hiring over the coming four quarters.

I chose to keep all 125 affected people employed and to avoid eliminating any roles. The Company hires about 500 people a year from outside into production, maintenance and warehouse roles, so moving existing staff into those roles fills real openings, gives affected employees a path to continued work, and avoids the severance cost and the loss of experience that elimination brings. Retraining at $15,000 a person pays back in two years against outside hiring, so the move is also sound for shareholders.

I split the group between two retraining paths. 85 people move at plant-role pay. For most of them, mainly office and administrative support staff, the pay reduction is small (about 1.5%), and the Company avoids any recurring top-up cost. For business and financial operations staff the reduction is large (about 39.8%), which is hard on those employees, so I placed 40 people on the path that keeps current pay. That path carries a recurring cost of roughly $0.66 million a year for these 40, plus one-time retraining and training wages. The Company can fund it from the $44.1 million of cash above the minimum operating level and from free cash flow of $166.5 million, and it does not affect dividends or the capital program.

Overall the decision saves the same $11.4 million a year in roles as every path does, keeps customers served by experienced staff, protects most employees' income, supports the communities where the plants sit, and keeps shareholder returns intact. The board should review the top-up cost and the pay outcomes for the 85 people at plant pay after four quarters.

We are removing the work of 125 roles, 70 in office and administrative support and 55 in business and financial operations, whatever happens to the people in them. The aim is to remove that work while keeping as many people employed as is sound for the Company, its customers, its shareholders and the people affected.

I have chosen 100 people for retraining into plant roles at plant pay. The plants hire about 500 people a year from outside into roles that these employees can fill after retraining. Retraining costs $15,000 each and pays back within two years against outside hiring, so this path fills a real need at lower cost than hiring. The pay change is small for office and administrative staff (1.5%), but large for business and financial operations staff (39.8%), so this path carries real harm for some of them, and I accept that as the price of keeping them employed.

I have chosen 15 people to retrain and keep their current pay. This protects those most exposed to the large pay cut, most likely from business and financial operations, at an ongoing cost of about $16,560 each per year, roughly $0.25 million a year for this group. That is affordable against the $44.1 million of cash above the minimum operating level.

I have chosen 10 people for elimination of their role with severance, about $8,902 each, roughly $0.09 million in total. I keep this path small because it ends employment, and I use it only for a limited group. Severance is cheap, but it is the path most damaging to employees, so I keep it to the minimum that the other paths do not absorb.

Total one-time cost is about $7.5 million for retraining and about $5.7 million in pay during training for the 115 retrained, plus severance. Every path is funded from existing cash. The eliminated work saves $11.4 million a year with benefits on every path, so the decision is financially sound and protects most jobs.

I decided to move most of the 125 affected people into plant roles, with a small group on current pay and a small group eliminated with severance.

Reasoning: the plants hire about 500 people a year from outside, so redeploying these employees fills roles the Company would otherwise fill by hiring. That makes the $15,000 retraining cost pay back in two years and keeps experienced people employed. Moving at plant pay costs about $60,600 per person once (retraining plus six months of pay during training). The pay cut is small for office and administrative staff (1.5%, about $839 a year), so most of that group can move without hardship. The cut is severe for business and financial operations staff (39.8%, about $36,569 a year), so I kept a group on current pay for those most exposed. Keeping current pay carries a recurring top-up of about $16,560 per person a year, so I limited that group to 10 people, roughly $166,000 a year in total, rather than the $2.1 million a year it would cost for everyone.

I kept 10 people on severance for those who may prefer to leave. Severance is the cheapest one-off option, about $8,902 each, and it respects individual choice.

Total one-off cost is roughly $7.3 million, well within the $44.1 million of cash above the minimum operating level. The eliminated roles save $11.4 million a year with benefits, as the work is no longer needed, and the Company keeps that saving on every path. The split supports employees, plants, customers who need continuity of service, and shareholders, because the Company avoids the cost of hiring from outside and keeps skills in the business. The allocation should be reviewed after the next four quarters, once we see how many people accept plant roles and how the pay gap affects retention.

Decision: 105 people move to plant roles keeping their current pay; 20 take severance; none take the plant-pay path.

Reasoning. The 125 roles can be removed on every path, so the $11.4 million annual saving is secured regardless. The choice is how the affected people are treated and what it costs the Company. The Company hires about 500 people a year from outside into plant roles, so retrained staff fill positions that would otherwise be filled externally. That gives retraining real value and means the workers are placed into genuine demand.

Keeping current pay costs about $2.1 million a year in pay differences, plus a one-time $1.9 million for retraining and $5.7 million of pay during training. Against $44.1 million of cash above the minimum, $238.5 million of operating income and $166.5 million of free cash flow, that is affordable. It keeps 105 families' incomes intact, which is the strongest outcome for employees and for the communities where the plants sit.

The plant-pay path cuts pay by 39.8% for business and financial operations staff (about $36,600 a year). That is a severe harm to employees and would likely cause attrition and loss of morale, so I rejected it, even though it is cheaper per year than keeping pay.

Severance for 20 people is a voluntary exit for those who would rather leave. It costs about $0.2 million once (20 times $8,902), and it respects individual choice. The eliminate path is cheapest for shareholders but I limited it to a minority, since it ends income for those who do not choose it.

Trade-off: the ongoing $2.1 million pay top-up reduces margin modestly, a cost I judge justified by the stakeholder gains and the value of filling real plant vacancies. The board should monitor the top-up as an ongoing cost and review it against plant hiring and attrition over the coming year.

Decision: 10 roles eliminated with severance, 60 retrained into plant roles keeping current pay, 55 retrained into plant roles at plant pay.

Rationale: The 125 roles are work that AI tools can now absorb, so the $11.4 million annual saving is realized on every path. The question is how to treat the people. Retraining into plant roles is the strongest option for employees and for the Company. The plants hire about 500 people a year from outside, so each internal move fills a role that would otherwise go to a new hire, and the retraining cost of $15,000 per person pays back within two years against that hiring. Retraining keeps experienced people employed and preserves institutional knowledge, which serves employees, the community, and customers who depend on continuity in service.

I split the retrained group by how much each person would lose. Business and financial operations staff face a 39.8% pay cut on plant-role pay, which is a severe harm, so the larger share of retrained people keep current pay, funded from the $44.1 million of spare cash. Office and administrative staff face only a 1.5% cut at plant pay, so most of them move at plant pay, which is the cheaper path and carries a small, acceptable reduction.

I kept 10 roles as eliminations, where severance at about $8,902 per person is the sensible outcome for people unlikely to fit plant work, and to limit the recurring pay-difference cost. This keeps the recurring cost of the keep-pay path to a manageable level. Shareholders keep most of the saving and the dividend and buyback commitments remain covered by free cash flow. The mix balances employee protection, community employment, customer continuity, and financial discipline over the coming four quarters.

I have decided that all 125 affected people (70 in office and administrative support, 55 in business and financial operations) will be retrained and moved into plant roles, keeping their current pay for as long as they hold those roles.

The reasoning is based on the objective to create value for all stakeholders over the next four quarters, not only shareholders. Eliminating roles would end the pay of 125 people and leave them with a one-time severance of about $8,900 each, the worst outcome for employees and their communities, and I do not think the savings justify it when a better path is affordable. Moving at plant-role pay would avoid that, but it cuts business and financial operations staff's pay by 39.8%, about $36,600 a year each. That is a severe hardship imposed on people whose jobs are being redesigned through no fault of their own, and I am not willing to impose it when the Company can afford to avoid it.

Keeping current pay costs about $2.1 million a year in pay differences, plus $1.9 million in retraining and $5.7 million in pay during the six-month training. The total one-time cost is about $7.6 million, and the recurring cost is about $2.1 million a year. Cash above the minimum operating level is $44.1 million, so this is fundable from existing cash. It reduces the cash available for dividends and repurchases, and I accept that trade-off, since shareholders still receive a return and the Company keeps its investment in its workforce.

The plants hire about 500 people a year from outside into production, maintenance and warehouse roles. Filling those roles internally, with 125 people who already know the Company, is worth more than hiring and training strangers, and it supports the retraining payback of about two years. The work removed by AI, $11.4 million a year, is saved on every path, so the decision does not depend on it.

I will monitor the pay differences, the retraining results and the plant hiring need over the year, and I will report back on whether this path continues to deliver value to employees, customers and communities as well as to shareholders.

I decided how to place the 125 people whose roles AI tools can take over, in office and administrative support (70) and business and financial operations (55). The $11.4 million a year of work cost is saved on every path, so the choice turns on people, cost and the plants' hiring needs.

I chose 85 people to be retrained and moved into plant roles at plant pay. The plants hire about 500 people a year from outside, so these moves fill real openings and avoid external hiring. Retraining costs $60,600 per person once (instruction plus training pay), which pays back in two years against outside hiring. Keeping these people employed supports the workforce and the communities where the plants sit. Office staff face only a 1.5% pay cut on this path, which is modest.

I chose 25 people to be moved keeping their current pay. This protects the business and financial staff, who would otherwise take a 39.8% pay cut, and cushions those most affected. The recurring cost is roughly $16,560 per person a year, about $0.4 million a year for these 25, which I judge acceptable for the protection it gives.

I chose 15 people to have their roles eliminated with severance, about $8,902 each, or roughly $0.13 million in total. This keeps the recurring cost of the keep-pay path contained and gives those who prefer separation a clean exit, and it fits the plant capacity actually available to us.

Total one-time cost is well within the $44.1 million of cash above the minimum operating level. This mix balances employee welfare, customer and community continuity, and cost discipline for shareholders over the next four quarters.

Decision: no roles are eliminated. 100 of the 125 affected people are retrained and moved into plant roles at plant pay; 25 are retrained and moved into plant roles keeping their current pay.

Reasoning: The objective asks for value across customers, employees, suppliers, communities and shareholders. Eliminating roles would end income for 125 people and is the outcome least consistent with that objective, so I have avoided it. The retraining paths keep these people employed in the plants, which need about 500 hires a year from outside anyway, so the retrained workers fill roles the Company would otherwise hire for.

Plant-pay retraining costs about $60,600 per person once (instruction, materials and training pay), which the Company recovers in about two years against outside hiring. For 100 people that is roughly $6.1 million once. The pay reduction is small for office and administrative staff (1.5%) but large for business and financial operations staff (39.8%). Keeping current pay for 25 people protects the staff facing the largest cut. The premium is about $16,560 per person per year, or about $0.4 million a year for 25 people, which is affordable from the $44.1 million of cash above minimum operating level and does not require new borrowing.

Total one-time cost is roughly $7.6 million, and the $11.4 million annual saving from the removed work is kept on every path. Cash stays above the minimum operating level.

Trade-offs: the keep-pay premium is a continuing cost that reduces the saving, and the 25 people on it will need reviewing as their plant roles settle. Pay cuts remain for most of the business and financial staff on the plant-pay path, and we should monitor morale, retention and the retraining outcomes over the next four quarters, and revisit the split if these fall short.

I decided to retrain most of the 125 affected people into plant roles, since the plants hire about 500 people a year from outside and these retrained employees would fill roles the Company needs filled anyway. Ninety people take the plant-pay path. Retraining costs $15,000 each, once, and the training pay of about $45,600 is paid once; the cost is recovered in about two years against outside hiring, and the employees keep working and earning. Their income falls on average, most sharply for business and financial operations staff (39.8%), so I want the board to see that as a real harm.

I put 25 people on the keep-pay path to cushion that effect for those who would otherwise face the largest cut. The trade-off is a recurring pay-difference cost of about $16,560 per person per year, roughly $0.4 million a year for these 25, which is affordable from existing cash and reduces the financial case for the program, but it protects employees' income and reduces the risk of losing experienced staff.

I kept 10 people on severance. Severance costs about $8,902 each, once, and some employees may prefer to leave or may not suit plant work. Eliminating these roles saves their full pay and benefits. I kept this group small because forced job loss carries real costs for employees and their communities, and because the plants' hiring need is best met by retraining.

Total one-time cost is modest and fully covered by existing cash above the minimum operating level. The mix balances the Company's ongoing cost, the value of retaining experienced people, the needs of the plants, and the wellbeing of employees, while the savings on the eliminated work ($11.4 million a year) are captured on every path.

Decision: no roles eliminated; 25 people retrained into plant roles keeping current pay; 100 retrained into plant roles at plant pay.

Reasoning. The roughly 25% of work in office and administrative support and business and financial operations that AI can now take over is removed whatever happens to the 125 people, so the $11.4 million saving is secured on every path. The question is how the people are treated. Eliminating all 125 would save severance-cheap upfront ($1.1 million) but would end employment for people the Company can instead place, and it would forgo the value of filling about 500 plant hires a year that would otherwise come from outside. Retraining into plant roles does that at a one-time cost of about $15,000 plus $45,600 of training pay per person, which pays back within two years against external hiring.

Plant pay is the durable choice for most. For office and administrative staff the pay change is small (1.5%), so 100 people take it. Business and financial operations staff face a 39.8% cut on plant pay, which is a severe hardship, so the Company keeps current pay for a smaller group of 25 for as long as they hold plant roles. That recurring differential, about $16,560 a person on average, costs roughly $0.4 million a year for this group, affordable within the savings and the $44.1 million of cash above the minimum.

Trade-offs. The keep-pay path carries an open-ended cost, and I have limited it to a minority. The board should monitor the differential and the plant roles' retention. Customers are served by retained, retrained staff who know the Company's products; suppliers keep their volume; shareholders bear a modest, one-time training cost and a bounded recurring cost against a permanent saving on the removed work. All amounts are funded from existing cash, leaving the minimum operating balance intact.

I chose not to eliminate any of the 125 roles. Severance would end the pay of people who could otherwise keep working for the Company, and it would bring no benefit to employees or communities. The Company also already hires about 500 people a year from outside into plant roles, so moving affected staff into those roles avoids external hiring costs. On the Company's own estimate, the $60,600 cost per retrained person is paid back within two years.

I split the group between the two retraining paths according to how much each path costs the individual. For the 85 people moved at plant-role pay, the average pay cut is small for office and administrative staff (1.5%), so they keep steady work at a modest reduction. Business and financial operations staff face a 39.8% cut on plant-role pay, which is a serious hardship. I therefore placed 40 people, weighted toward that group, on the path that keeps current pay. The top-up is about $0.66 million a year for the 40 people, which is affordable within the $44.1 million of cash above the minimum operating level, and it protects the people most exposed to the pay cut.

Total one-time retraining cost for 125 people is about $7.6 million, plus wages during training of about $5.7 million, which are paid while staff remain on payroll. The saving on the eliminated work of $11.4 million a year is realised on every path. Cash remains above the minimum after these costs, and no debt is needed.

This allocation weighs employees' livelihoods against the Company's cost base and gives shareholders a return on the retraining investment. It does not fully protect every person from pay reduction, and the ongoing top-up is a continuing cost that the board should monitor each year.

I decided that 95 of the 125 people should be retrained and moved into plant roles at plant-role pay, 20 should be retrained and moved into plant roles keeping their current pay, and 10 should have their roles eliminated with severance.

The main reason is that the Company hires about 500 people a year from outside into production, maintenance and warehouse roles. That gives the plant-pay path real value for the Company, for shareholders, and for the communities where the plants operate, since it keeps experienced people employed.

For employees, the plant-pay path is a small cut for office and administrative staff (about 1.5%) but a large one for business and financial operations staff (about 40%). Its cost is recurring, about $16,560 per person a year, so I limited it to 20 people, about $0.3 million a year, rather than the full $2.1 million a year it would cost if all 125 took it.

Severance for 10 people is the path with the lowest immediate cash cost, about $8,900 each, and it reflects that some people may prefer to leave. It also keeps some flexibility if placements into plant roles prove harder than expected.

The one-time cash cost is roughly $7.0 million for retraining and pay during training, plus under $0.1 million in severance. This is well within the $44.1 million of cash above the minimum operating level. The annual savings of $11.4 million from the work no longer being needed apply on every path.

The split is a judgment that balances value to shareholders, the retention of jobs for employees, and the Company's continued access to skilled plant labor.

I chose to retrain all 125 affected people into plant roles rather than eliminate any roles. I will monitor the retention and productivity of retrained staff over the next four quarters and revisit the split if the top-up cost or the performance of the plants changes.

I chose to move 75 of the 125 affected people into plant roles at plant pay and to eliminate 50 roles with severance. No one takes the keep-current-pay path.

Why redeploy 75: the plants hire about 500 people a year from outside into production, maintenance and warehouse roles. Filling some of those openings from within the affected group avoids external hiring, and retraining at $15,000 a person pays back in about two years. It keeps experienced people employed, which serves employees and the communities where the plants sit.

Why not keep current pay: that path adds $2.1 million a year in recurring cost for all 125. With only $44.1 million of cash above the minimum and $146.1 million a year already paid to shareholders, I do not think the Company should take on that permanent cost. Pay gaps of this size would be hard to sustain once the retraining period ends.

Why eliminate 50: the plant-pay cut is small for office and administrative staff (1.5%) but very large for business and financial operations staff (39.8%). For the latter, severance at 1.5 weeks per year of service, with a median of 4.3 years in the industry, gives a real cushion, and a near-40% pay cut is harsher than a clean exit. I applied the split in proportion to each function's headcount, so the moves are 42 office and 33 business and financial, and the eliminations are 28 office and 22 business and financial.

Trade-offs: the eliminations end income for 50 people, and the Company bears a one-time retraining cost for 75. The Company still saves the $11.4 million a year in cost for this work on every path. Customers are not affected by these choices. Suppliers are not affected. Shareholders receive the savings net of one-time costs. I will track how the redeployed staff perform and whether pay cuts cause attrition, and I will revisit the mix if either goes badly.

I chose to keep all 125 people employed rather than eliminate any roles. Severance would save cash up front ($1.1 million) but would end the livelihoods of 125 employees and their families and weaken the Company's standing in its communities, which runs against the objective to create value for all stakeholders.

I accepted it for this group because the pay loss otherwise would be very large.

The split is a balance among employees, customers and shareholders: people keep jobs where the pay change is tolerable, the most exposed workers are protected at a cost I judge acceptable, and the Company avoids paying ongoing pay differences across the whole group. Every path is funded from existing cash above the minimum operating level. I will review the keep-pay group each year against the cost to shareholders.

I decided that none of the 125 affected people should be eliminated. Severance is cheap (about $1.1 million in total), but it ends pay for 125 people and sends them into the local labor market while the Company is hiring about 500 people a year into plant roles that these employees could fill after retraining. Retraining keeps people employed, uses their institutional knowledge of the Company, and avoids the community harm of job loss.

Among the retraining paths, I split the group. The plant-pay path costs the same one-time amount (about $60,600 a person including training pay) and has no recurring premium, which protects cash and shareholder value. However, it cuts business and financial operations pay by 39.8%, a hardship I am not willing to impose on everyone in that group. The keep-pay path protects their pay, but it adds about $2.1 million a year if all 125 took it, which is a lasting drain on cash and returns.

So I placed 35 people on the keep-pay path, weighted toward business and financial operations staff whose plant-role pay would fall most sharply, and 90 on the plant-pay path, mainly office and administrative staff, whose pay falls only 1.5%. This keeps the recurring cost to roughly $0.6 million a year, well within available cash of $44.1 million above minimum operating levels, and it still captures most of the value of filling plant hiring needs internally.

The one-time retraining cost for 125 people is about $7.6 million, funded from existing cash. The elimination of the 125 roles saves $11.4 million a year. The split is applied in the same proportion across both functions, as the board pack requires. I will review the keep-pay population each year to see whether pay gaps can close as people gain experience in plant roles.
